strengths: The paper proposes a very simple and appealing regularizer: align early diffusion-transformer representations to later-layer representations with a stop-gradient cosine loss. The method is easy to implement, parameter-free, and does not require external pretrained representation models.

The main ImageNet 256x256 results are strong. LayerSync consistently improves SiT-B/L/XL across training budgets, outperforms the most relevant self-contained baseline, Dispersive Loss, and reaches competitive CFG performance relative to recent transformer diffusion methods.

The paper makes a credible effort to test generality beyond images, with additional experiments on audio, human motion, and video generation. The consistent direction of improvements across modalities supports the claim that the idea is not purely image-specific.

The representation analysis is useful: linear probing, segmentation probing, and CKA suggest that the method improves intermediate features rather than merely changing sample metrics. The layer-selection and lambda ablations are also helpful and show some robustness.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The core idea is essentially internal feature self-distillation across layers, and the paper does not sufficiently position itself against broader self-distillation, auxiliary representation alignment, FitNets-style hints, BYOL/SimSiam-like stop-gradient alignment, or the cited 2025 work claiming diffusion transformers can provide their own representation guidance.

The evidence outside ImageNet is comparatively thin. Audio and motion lack strong baselines beyond the vanilla model, appear to use single runs, and rely only on aggregate metrics. Video results are placed in the appendix, use short fine-tuning or short from-scratch runs, and do not establish whether gains persist at scale or with stronger training budgets.

The claim of “no overhead” is overstated. Even without extra forward passes or parameters, extracting/storing intermediate activations and computing the alignment loss has memory and compute costs; the paper reports only asymptotic comparison to Dispersive Loss, not actual wall-clock throughput, memory usage, or end-to-end training cost.

The “8.75x acceleration” framing is somewhat fragile: it is based on matching a particular FID between SiT-XL trained for 1400 epochs and LayerSync trained for 160 epochs, while other comparisons use different samplers and guidance settings. More careful compute-normalized comparisons would strengthen the claim.

The ablations leave important questions unresolved: why specific target layers work, whether aligning multiple pairs helps or hurts, whether the stop-gradient direction matters, whether cosine similarity is essential, and whether the method can collapse or over-constrain representations in longer training.

Reproducibility is incomplete for a top-tier submission. The paper says code will be released upon acceptance, but the abstract’s code link appears blank, and several experiments require large compute. Missing details such as random seeds, variance for main results, actual training time, and evaluation scripts limit confidence.

strengths: The paper studies an important problem: improving training efficiency and generation quality of diffusion/flow models without relying on external representation teachers.

The proposed LayerSync objective is simple, easy to integrate into transformer-based generative models, and conceptually appealing: use later-layer representations as stop-gradient targets for earlier layers.
The empirical scope is broad, covering image, audio, human motion, and video generation, with generally consistent improvements over the authors' chosen vanilla and Dispersive Loss baselines.
The image-generation experiments include multiple SiT model sizes and several training budgets, and the paper provides useful ablations for layer selection and the regularization coefficient.
The representation analysis using linear probing, segmentation probing, and CKA provides some evidence that the method affects internal features rather than only final sample metrics.
weaknesses: The novelty is not strong enough for a top-tier AI conference. Aligning shallow and deep representations within the same network is a natural variant of self-distillation/deep supervision/feature matching, and the paper does not sufficiently distinguish LayerSync from very close internal representation guidance methods, including the cited Jiang et al. 2025 work.

The main technical claim of being zero-overhead or no-overhead is insufficiently supported. Computing and storing intermediate representations plus an additional alignment loss is not free; the paper reports FLOP scaling only in a simplified comparison to Dispersive Loss, but does not provide wall-clock, memory, throughput, or end-to-end compute comparisons.

The evaluation is weaker than the broad claims suggest. Most comparisons are against vanilla SiT and Dispersive Loss; stronger self-distillation, auxiliary-loss, representation-regularization, and deep-supervision baselines are missing. The system-level ImageNet table also shows LayerSync is not competitive with several externally guided or stronger architecture baselines, despite some claims sounding close to state of the art.

Several experimental comparisons are potentially unfair or hard to interpret. Speedup is mostly reported in epochs or iterations rather than actual training compute; audio uses a very large 64-GPU setup but lacks meaningful baselines; video results are relegated to the appendix with short fine-tuning runs and limited detail; motion improvements are small and reported without variance.

The claimed domain-agnostic generality is not fully established. The non-image experiments appear to use different metrics, architectures, similarity losses, and limited baselines, so they read more as preliminary demonstrations than convincing evidence of a general principle.

Reproducibility is limited. The code is only promised upon acceptance, and important details for reproducing large-scale runs, non-image setups, sampling protocols, hyperparameter searches, and evaluation pipelines are either sparse or scattered. This is a concern given the large compute requirements and metric sensitivity.

The paper overstates some conclusions. For example, the representation analysis compares a 160-epoch LayerSync model to a 1400-epoch baseline with similar FID, but this does not cleanly isolate the regularizer's effect from optimization trajectory, model state, or training-time differences. Claims about recursive refinement and fundamentally altered optimization are speculative.

There is limited robustness analysis. The paper does not adequately study failure cases, long-training behavior, sensitivity to architecture families beyond transformer diffusion models, effects on diversity beyond standard FID/precision/recall, or possible layer collapse/pathological alignment.
Presentation quality is uneven, with typos, formatting issues, and some imprecise statements. These do not by themselves determine the score, but they reinforce concerns about rigor and polish.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple, elegant, and practically useful regularizer: aligning weaker early diffusion-model layers to stronger internal layers with stop-gradient, avoiding external pretrained guidance models or additional data.

The main empirical results are strong. On ImageNet 256x256, LayerSync consistently improves FID across SiT-B/L/XL scales and across training budgets, and substantially outperforms the closest self-contained baseline, Dispersive Loss.
The work is unusually broad for this topic, with evidence beyond images on audio, human motion, and video generation, supporting the claim that the idea is not purely vision-specific.
The method has low implementation complexity and appears computationally attractive relative to external-representation guidance and pairwise representation regularizers.

The representation analysis is a valuable addition: linear probing, segmentation probing, and CKA suggest that LayerSync changes the learned feature hierarchy rather than only improving sample metrics.
Ablations on layer choice and lambda provide useful evidence that the method is relatively robust and not extremely dependent on a fragile hyperparameter search.
weaknesses: The novelty is meaningful but incremental: the core mechanism is a straightforward internal feature distillation/alignment loss, and the paper would benefit from sharper positioning against recent self-guidance and teacher-student representation regularization methods, especially Jiang et al. 2025 and related internal representation guidance work.

The strongest comparisons are in image generation; the audio, motion, and video experiments are more limited, often comparing mainly against vanilla and Dispersive rather than strong domain-specific baselines or external-guidance analogues.

The claim of 'no overhead' is somewhat overstated. While LayerSync needs no external model and no extra forward pass, it still adds feature normalization/similarity computation and may impose activation/memory considerations; wall-clock throughput or memory measurements would make this claim more convincing.

The paper reports many single-run results for expensive generative experiments. More variance estimates or repeated runs for the headline ImageNet, audio, motion, and video results would strengthen confidence in the gains.

Reproducibility is only promised upon acceptance; the current manuscript does not appear to provide released code or full configurations/checkpoints, which weakens verifiability for a top-tier submission.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, particularly around 'domain-agnostic' behavior and recursive/cascading feature refinement. The evidence is suggestive, but the underlying mechanism remains partly speculative.
The ethics statement is generic and does not seriously discuss the broader implications of making diffusion model training cheaper across image, audio, and video generation.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and appealing self-contained regularizer: aligning earlier diffusion-transformer layers to later internal representations with stop-gradient. The method is easy to understand, broadly applicable in principle, and does not require external pretrained guidance models or extra data.

The ImageNet experiments are extensive and impressive. LayerSync consistently improves SiT-B/L/XL across training budgets, outperforms Dispersive Loss, and remains competitive with stronger externally guided approaches when classifier-free guidance is used.

The paper includes useful ablations on layer-pair choice, regularization weight, timestep range, learning-rate alternatives, and combination with REPA. These go beyond a single headline result and support the claim that the gain is not just a trivial optimization-speed artifact.

The representation analysis is a valuable addition: linear probing, segmentation probing, CKA comparisons, and layer-evolution studies provide plausible evidence that the regularizer changes internal feature quality, not merely final FID.
The attempt to test the same idea across image, audio, motion, and video generation is a notable strength and supports the broader relevance of the approach.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. The core mechanism is a straightforward internal feature-distillation/consistency loss, and it is close in spirit to concurrent or related self-representation alignment methods such as SRA. The paper would benefit from sharper positioning around what is fundamentally new beyond using later layers as stop-gradient targets.

The claim of “no overhead” is overstated. Even if no new parameters or external forward pass are introduced, the method adds feature extraction/storage, similarity computation, and backpropagation through the shallow layer. The FLOP and wall-clock comparisons are limited and do not fully characterize memory cost or training throughput across the main experiments.

The strongest evidence is concentrated on ImageNet/SiT. The audio, motion, and video experiments are comparatively thin: they mostly compare a baseline to LayerSync, use limited metrics, and lack strong domain-specific baselines, multiple seeds, or deeper ablations. Thus the “domain-agnostic” claim is plausible but not fully established.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract has an unfinished code-availability statement, and the reproducibility section only promises code upon acceptance. Given the scale of the compute and the sensitivity of diffusion training, lack of released code/configs/checkpoints at review time weakens confidence.

Some comparisons in the system-level ImageNet table are hard to interpret because methods differ in architecture, training budget, sampler, CFG usage, guidance scheduling, and external-model dependence. The paper sometimes turns these heterogeneous comparisons into stronger state-of-the-art claims than the evidence warrants.

The layer-selection strategy still appears heuristic. Although the ablations are helpful, performance varies substantially for some layer pairs, and the paper does not provide a principled or automatic way to choose layers for new architectures or modalities.

Several claims are phrased too strongly relative to the evidence, especially the “virtuous cycle” explanation and assertions about fundamentally altering optimization trajectories. The empirical observations are suggestive, but not sufficient to establish the proposed mechanism causally.

strengths: The proposed regularizer is simple, parameter-free, and easy to integrate into diffusion-transformer training: align an earlier layer to a later layer with a stop-gradient cosine-similarity loss.

The ImageNet experiments report consistent FID improvements across SiT-B/L/XL and across training budgets, with useful ablations on layer choice, regularization weight, timestep conditioning, and learning-rate alternatives.
The paper includes representation analyses via linear probing, segmentation, CKA, and block-correlation structure, which help connect the method to its stated motivation.
The authors make an effort to test beyond images, with preliminary results on audio, motion, and video generation, suggesting the idea may have some modality-agnostic value.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. Inter-layer self-distillation/feature alignment is a well-established idea, and the paper does not sufficiently distinguish LayerSync from prior self-distillation, deep supervision, FitNet-style hint losses, or the closely related SRA-style internal representation guidance cited in the paper.

Several central claims are overstated. The method is repeatedly described as having 'no overhead' or 'zero cost', but it adds feature extraction, activation retention, normalization, and similarity computation; the paper only argues no extra forward pass, which is a weaker claim.

The broad domain-agnostic claim is weakly supported. Audio, motion, and video experiments compare mostly against vanilla training, use few datasets, provide limited metrics, and lack strong domain-specific baselines or ablations. The video result is explicitly a short proof-of-concept, yet it is used to support broad claims.

The comparison to external-guidance and EMA/self-alignment methods is not fully satisfying. SRA appears very close conceptually, and the paper’s discussion of it is mostly empirical rather than clarifying what is technically new or why the proposed method is preferable beyond cost.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a top-tier submission. The abstract says code is available but the link is missing, while the reproducibility statement only promises release upon acceptance. Many expensive experiments are hard to verify, and there is little reporting of seeds or variance for main results.

The evaluation mixes settings in ways that make some headline acceleration claims hard to interpret, including ODE vs. SDE sampling, classifier-free guidance vs. no guidance, different batch/GPU settings across main experiments and ablations, and comparisons to methods with different training/sampling recipes.

The method’s limitations are underexplored. It assumes comparable hidden dimensions and spatial/temporal token alignment across layers, may not apply cleanly to architectures with changing resolution or heterogeneous widths, and does not analyze failure cases, collapse risks, or when forcing early layers toward later layers is harmful.

The paper’s explanation sometimes goes beyond the evidence, especially the 'virtuous cycle' interpretation. The experiments show correlations between deeper targets and better representations, but do not establish the proposed causal optimization mechanism.

strengths: Simple, well-motivated, and practically appealing method: LayerSync adds an internal shallow-to-deep representation alignment loss without external models, extra parameters, or apparent training-time overhead.
Empirical results on ImageNet are strong and consistent across SiT-B/L/XL scales and training budgets, with substantial FID improvements over both vanilla SiT and Dispersive Loss.

The paper includes a broad experimental story: image generation, audio generation, human motion generation, video generation, representation probing, compatibility with REPA, layer-selection ablations, timestep ablations, and comparisons to EMA-based SRA.
The representation analyses are useful and support the central hypothesis that the method improves intermediate features rather than merely changing final sample quality.
The method is easy to understand and likely easy to implement, which increases its potential impact for diffusion/flow model training.
weaknesses: The core technical idea is quite simple and close in spirit to self-distillation, intermediate-layer alignment, and recent self-representation alignment methods; the novelty is more in the specific diffusion-model instantiation and empirical validation than in a fundamentally new principle.

Some broad domain-general claims are supported by relatively limited evidence: audio, motion, and video experiments use few baselines, appear to be mostly single-run, and lack richer modality-specific evaluations or qualitative/user studies.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: the abstract’s code link appears blank in the extracted manuscript, and the reproducibility statement only commits to releasing code after acceptance.

The strongest system-level ImageNet claims require careful qualification: LayerSync is very competitive, but some external-guidance or other generative systems still outperform it, and comparisons mix settings such as CFG scheduling, training epochs, and model families.

The paper would be stronger with more statistical reporting across seeds for the main results, wall-clock training comparisons, and a more precise accounting of memory/compute overhead despite the claim of negligible or zero overhead.
